claim: Appetitive and aversive visual learning assays for Drosophila were established that are comparable to widely used olfactory learning assays.
source: We established appetitive and aversive visual learning assays for Drosophila that are comparable to the widely used olfactory learning assays.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development of new behavioral assays as a primary methodological contribution.

claim: Visual and olfactory learning assays share critical features including sugar reward and electric shock punishment as reinforcing stimuli.
source: These assays share critical features, such as reinforcing stimuli (sugar reward and electric shock punishment), and allow direct comparison of the cellular requirements for visual and olfactory memories.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the shared features of the assays.

claim: The same subsets of dopamine neurons drive formation of both visual and olfactory memories.
source: We found that the same subsets of dopamine neurons drive formation of both sensory memories.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2-4.

claim: Distinct yet partially overlapping subsets of mushroom body intrinsic neurons are required for visual and olfactory memories.
source: Furthermore, distinct yet partially overlapping subsets of mushroom body intrinsic neurons are required for visual and olfactory memories.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 5-8.

claim: Distinct sensory memories are processed in a common brain center (the mushroom body).
source: Thus, our results suggest that distinct sensory memories are processed in a common brain center.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing shared MB circuits.

claim: Centralization of related brain functions is an economical design that avoids repetition of similar circuit motifs.
source: Such centralization of related brain functions is an economical design that avoids the repetition of similar circuit motifs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: A traumatic event drives aversive associative memories of concurrent auditory and visual stimuli in rats.
source: For example, a traumatic event drives aversive associative memories of concurrent auditory and visual stimuli in rats (Campeau and Davis, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The same appetitive and aversive reinforcers drive both olfactory and visual memories in insects.
source: The same appetitive and aversive reinforcers drive both olfactory and visual memories in insects, while associative memories with different modalities are formed using the same neurotransmitter system (Unoki et al., 2005, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in insects.

claim: The circuit mechanisms underlying memories of different sensory modalities driven by the same reinforcing stimulus are unknown.
source: However, the circuit mechanisms underlying memories of different sensory modalities driven by the same reinforcing stimulus are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Mushroom bodies are required for olfactory and gustatory memories in Drosophila.
source: For example, the mushroom bodies (MBs) are required for olfactory and gustatory memories (Heisenberg et al., 1985; Davis, 1993; Heisenberg, 2003; Masek and Scott, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: According to previous studies, mushroom bodies are not required for a visual memory task.
source: but according to previous studies, not for a visual memory task (Heisenberg et al., 1985; Wolf et al., 1998; Tang and Guo, 2001; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work showing no MB requirement for visual memory.

claim: Other studies suggest that visual information is indeed processed in the mushroom bodies.
source: Nevertheless, other studies suggest that visual information is indeed processed in the MBs (Barth and Heisenberg, 1997; Liu et al., 1999; Brembs and Wiener, 2006; van Swinderen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work suggesting MB involvement in visual processing.

claim: A transparent shock grid was fabricated from indium tin-oxide (ITO) to enable electric shock punishment during visual conditioning.
source: We solved this problem by fabricating a shock grid from a transparent low-resistance material, indium tin-oxide (ITO; Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the technical solution and references Figure 1 showing the apparatus.

claim: Electric shock served as potent aversive reinforcement and induced aversive visual memory at a signal to noise ratio comparable to visual memories in other paradigms.
source: The electric shock served as potent aversive reinforcement and induced aversive visual memory at a signal to noise ratio comparable to visual memories in other paradigms (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Menne and Spatz, 1977; Wolf and Heisenberg, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1F and comparison to cited prior work.

claim: Conditioned avoidance increased with ascending voltages and reached a plateau at approximately 30 V.
source: We found that conditioned avoidance increased with ascending voltages. A plateau was reached at approximately 30 V, and the performance did not change with more intense shock (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 60 V was applied for all subsequent aversive conditioning experiments.
source: Thus, we applied 60 V for all subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the voltage response data.

claim: A single shock pulse was applied 5 s before the beginning of the test to arouse the flies in aversive conditioning.
source: For aversive conditioning, a single shock pulse was applied 5 s before the beginning of the test to arouse the flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Menne and Spatz, 1977; Gerber and Hendel, 2006).
evidence: This methodological detail is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citations.

claim: Blocking octopamine/tyramine neurons with TDC2-GAL4 did not cause a significant defect in sucrose reward or shock punishment memory.
source: Blocking octopamine/tyramine neurons with TDC2-GAL4 did not cause a significant defect in sucrose reward or shock punishment memory (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Blockade of a large fraction of dopamine neurons with TH-GAL4 selectively reduced aversive memory.
source: In contrast, the blockade of a large fraction of dopamine neurons with TH-GAL4 selectively reduced aversive memory (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Blockade with DDC-GAL4 substantially impaired appetitive memory, but not aversive memory.
source: As in olfactory learning (Liu et al., 2012), the blockade with DDC-GAL4 that labels different sets of dopamine and serotonin neurons substantially impaired appetitive memory, but not aversive memory (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2A and comparison to cited prior work in olfactory learning.

claim: Blockade with DDC-GAL4 did not significantly affect the reflexive choice of sugar.
source: The blockade with DDC-GAL4 did not significantly affect the reflexive choice of sugar, while blocking the dopamine system with TH-GAL4 caused prolonged hyperactivity that indirectly influenced shock avoidance (Lebestky et al., 2009; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Table 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: Blocking the dopamine system with TH-GAL4 caused prolonged hyperactivity that indirectly influenced shock avoidance.
source: The blockade with DDC-GAL4 did not significantly affect the reflexive choice of sugar, while blocking the dopamine system with TH-GAL4 caused prolonged hyperactivity that indirectly influenced shock avoidance (Lebestky et al., 2009; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Table 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: Output of DDC-GAL4 labeled neurons is only necessary in appetitive training but dispensable during test.
source: The blockade with DDC-GAL4 during training severely impaired appetitive memory, whereas the same blockade after the training did not significantly affect memory (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal requirement data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Neurons labeled in TH-GAL4 were required specifically during acquisition of aversive memory.
source: Similarly, the neurons labeled in TH-GAL4 were required specifically during acquisition of aversive memory (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal requirement data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: The neurons differentially labeled with DDC-GAL4 and TH-GAL4 mediate the formation of appetitive and aversive visual memories, likely acting as reinforcement signals.
source: These results suggest that the neurons differentially labeled with DDC-GAL4 and TH-GAL4 mediate the formation of appetitive and aversive visual memories, likely acting as reinforcement signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal requirement data.

claim: Specific subsets of dopamine neurons in TH-GAL4 and DDC-GAL4 signal sugar reward and shock punishment for olfactory memories.
source: As specific subsets of dopamine neurons in TH-GAL4 and DDC-GAL4 have been shown to signal sugar reward and shock punishment for olfactory memories (Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on olfactory memory.

claim: R58E02-GAL4 drives GAL4 expression in the PAM cluster neurons that signal reward for olfactory memory.
source: R58E02-GAL4 drives GAL4 expression in the PAM cluster neurons that signal reward for olfactory memory (Figure 3A,C; Liu, et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 3A,C and citation to prior work.

claim: R58E02-GAL4 co-expresses with DDC-GAL4, but rarely with TH-GAL4, in the PAM cluster.
source: This driver co-expresses with DDC-GAL4, but rarely with TH-GAL4, in the PAM cluster (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work characterizing the driver.

claim: MB504B is a Split GAL4 line that specifically labels four individual dopamine neurons in the PPL1 cluster: MB-MP1, MB-MV1, MB-V1, and the neuron that projects to the tip of the α lobe.
source: MB504B is a Split GAL4 line we generated to specifically label four individual dopamine neurons in the PPL1 cluster: MB-MP1, MB-MV1, MB-V1, and the neuron that projects to the tip of the α lobe (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim describes a new genetic tool generated for this study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PPL1 cluster neurons labeled by MB504B have been shown to induce aversive olfactory memory.
source: These neurons are a subset of TH-GAL4 and have been shown, using a less specific line, to induce aversive olfactory memory (Aso et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Blockade of R58E02-GAL4 neurons with shibirets1 impaired appetitive visual memory.
source: We found that the blockade of these neurons with shits1 indeed impaired aversive or appetitive visual memory, respectively (Figure 3C–F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Blockade of MB504B-GAL4 neurons with shibirets1 impaired aversive visual memory.
source: We found that the blockade of these neurons with shits1 indeed impaired aversive or appetitive visual memory, respectively (Figure 3C–F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Blockade of R58E02-GAL4 and MB504B-GAL4 neurons did not significantly affect the reflexive choice of sugar and shock.
source: but did not significantly affect the reflexive choice of sugar and shock (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control data in Table 1.

claim: Visual and olfactory memories share neuronal substrates for appetitive and aversive reinforcements.
source: Thus, we conclude that visual and olfactory memories share neuronal substrates for appetitive and aversive reinforcements.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the shared requirement of specific dopamine neuron subsets.

claim: Thermo-activation of the PAM cluster neurons with R58E02-GAL4 was sufficient to induce appetitive memory.
source: Thermo-activation of the PAM and PPL1 cluster neurons with R58E02-GAL4 and MB504B-GAL4 was sufficient to induce appetitive and aversive memories, respectively (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Thermo-activation of the PPL1 cluster neurons with MB504B-GAL4 was sufficient to induce aversive memory.
source: Thermo-activation of the PAM and PPL1 cluster neurons with R58E02-GAL4 and MB504B-GAL4 was sufficient to induce appetitive and aversive memories, respectively (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Different subsets of dopamine neurons supply appetitive and aversive reinforcement information for visual as well as olfactory memories.
source: Based on these results we conclude that different subsets of dopamine neurons supply appetitive and aversive reinforcement information for visual as well as olfactory memories.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the thermo-activation and blockade experiments.

claim: DopR, a D1-like dopamine receptor, is required for olfactory memories.
source: Since DopR, a D1-like dopamine receptor, is required for olfactory memories (Kim et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The dumb2 mutant for DopR shows severe appetitive and aversive visual memory defects.
source: Consistent with our results from the block of dopamine neurons, we found severe appetitive and aversive visual memory defects in the mutant for DopR (dumb2; Kim et al., 2007, Figure 4D, see Table 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for controls).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: Selective expression of DopR+ in the Kenyon cells using MB247-GAL4 significantly rescued the memory defect of the dumb2 mutant.
source: Selective expression of DopR+ in the KCs using MB247-GAL4 significantly rescued the memory defect of the mutant (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The same sets of dopamine neurons convey reward and punishment signals to the mushroom bodies to induce appetitive and aversive memories of different sensory modalities.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the same sets of dopamine neurons convey reward and punishment signals to the MBs to induce appetitive and aversive memories of the different sensory modalities.
evidence: This conclusion integrates findings from dopamine neuron manipulation and DopR rescue experiments.

claim: Both appetitive and aversive visual memories were significantly impaired when Kenyon cells were blocked with 201y-GAL4 and MB247-GAL4.
source: Both appetitive and aversive memories in the experimental groups were significantly impaired (Figure 5A, see Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for controls).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of MB247-GAL80 fully restored the impaired memories caused by 201y-GAL4 blockade.
source: Addition of MB247-GAL80 fully restored the impaired memories (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Visual memories require the output of Kenyon cells.
source: Thus, we conclude that visual memories require the output of KCs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the blockade and rescue experiments.

claim: Visual memory in the assay requires the mushroom bodies independent of the conditioning design (classical vs operant) and of context changes between training and test.
source: Thus we conclude that visual memory in our assay requires the MBs independent of the conditioning design (classical vs operant) and of context changes between training and test.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments with modified conditioning protocols shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Blocking the α′/β′ neurons with c305a-GAL4 selectively impaired olfactory memory but not visual memory.
source: Blocking the α′/β′ neurons with c305a-GAL4 selectively impaired olfactory memory (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Blockade with 17D-GAL4 (α/β neurons) had no significant perturbation of either visual or olfactory memory.
source: 17D-GAL4/shits1 flies had no significant perturbation of either memory, while the blockade of the α/β and γ neurons with 201y-GAL4 strongly impaired both visual and olfactory memories (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Blockade of the α/β and γ neurons with 201y-GAL4 strongly impaired both visual and olfactory memories.
source: 17D-GAL4/shits1 flies had no significant perturbation of either memory, while the blockade of the α/β and γ neurons with 201y-GAL4 strongly impaired both visual and olfactory memories (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Visual and olfactory memories recruit partially overlapping Kenyon cell subsets.
source: Hence, visual and olfactory memories recruit partially overlapping KC subsets.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential requirements of KC subsets shown in Figure 6.

claim: The specific contribution of αʹ/βʹ neurons to olfactory learning is consistent with the preferential representation of olfactory inputs to these neurons.
source: The specific contribution of αʹ/βʹ neurons to olfactory learning is consistent with the preferential representation of olfactory inputs to these neurons (Turner et al., 2008).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to prior work on olfactory input representation.

claim: Blocking the output of the γ lobe neurons (MB009B-GAL4) impaired both appetitive and aversive visual memories.
source: Blocking the output of the γ lobe neurons (Figures 7A, MB009B-GAL4, see Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for controls) as well as the entire KC population (Figures 7A, MB010B-GAL4, see Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for controls) impaired both appetitive and aversive visual memories (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Blocking the output of the entire Kenyon cell population (MB010B-GAL4) impaired both appetitive and aversive visual memories.
source: Blocking the output of the γ lobe neurons (Figures 7A, MB009B-GAL4, see Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for controls) as well as the entire KC population (Figures 7A, MB010B-GAL4, see Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for controls) impaired both appetitive and aversive visual memories (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Blocking the output of α′/β′ neurons (MB186B-GAL4) did not significantly reduce visual memory performance compared to controls.
source: Blocking the output of α′/β′ neurons (Figures 7A, MB186B-GAL4) or α/β neurons (Figures 7A, MB008B-GAL4) did not significantly reduce the performance compared to the controls (Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Blocking the output of α/β neurons (MB008B-GAL4) did not significantly reduce visual memory performance compared to controls.
source: Blocking the output of α′/β′ neurons (Figures 7A, MB186B-GAL4) or α/β neurons (Figures 7A, MB008B-GAL4) did not significantly reduce the performance compared to the controls (Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The required Kenyon cell subsets for appetitive and aversive visual memories were strikingly similar.
source: The required KC subsets for appetitive and aversive memories were strikingly similar.
evidence: This observation is drawn from comparing the results in Figure 7B.

claim: The output of specific subsets of Kenyon cells representing visual information is differentially modulated by reward or punishment.
source: This suggests that the output of specific subsets of KCs representing visual information is differentially modulated by reward or punishment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the similar KC requirements for appetitive and aversive memories.

claim: Output of Kenyon cells labeled by MB010B-GAL4 is necessary during aversive training and test.
source: We transiently blocked the output of a broad population of KCs using MB010B-GAL4 (Figure 8A–D, all lobes) (Bräcker et al., 2013) and MB247-GAL4 (Figure 8A,B,E,F; α/β and γ lobes) and found requirement for KCs in memory acquisition and retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal requirement data shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: Output of Kenyon cells labeled by MB247-GAL4 is necessary during aversive training and test.
source: We transiently blocked the output of a broad population of KCs using MB010B-GAL4 (Figure 8A–D, all lobes) (Bräcker et al., 2013) and MB247-GAL4 (Figure 8A,B,E,F; α/β and γ lobes) and found requirement for KCs in memory acquisition and retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal requirement data shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: Output of Kenyon cells labeled by 201y-GAL4 is dispensable during training but necessary during aversive test.
source: Interestingly, the transiently blocked output of a smaller set of KCs using 201y-GAL4 (α/β and γ lobes) and MB009B-GAL4 (γ lobes) revealed a selective requirement for the retrieval but not the formation of aversive visual memory (Figure 8A,B,G,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal requirement data shown in Figures 8G and 8H.

claim: Output of Kenyon cells labeled by MB009B-GAL4 is dispensable during training but necessary during aversive test.
source: Interestingly, the transiently blocked output of a smaller set of KCs using 201y-GAL4 (α/β and γ lobes) and MB009B-GAL4 (γ lobes) revealed a selective requirement for the retrieval but not the formation of aversive visual memory (Figure 8A,B,G,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal requirement data shown in Figures 8I and 8J.

claim: Output of Kenyon cells labeled by MB247-GAL4 is needed during appetitive training and test.
source: Output of KCs labeled by MB247-GAL4 (α/β and γ lobes) was also required for acquisition and retrieval of appetitive memory (Figure 8A,B,K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal requirement data shown in Figures 8K and 8L.

claim: Different Kenyon cells mediate acquisition and retrieval of visual memories.
source: We thus conclude that different KCs mediate acquisition and retrieval of visual memories.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential temporal requirements of KC subsets shown in Figure 8.

claim: Circuits underlying olfactory and visual memory can be optimally compared when the sugar reward and electric shock punishment are matched between the two modalities.
source: Circuits underlying olfactory and visual memory can be optimally compared when the sugar reward and electric shock punishment are matched between the two modalities.
evidence: This is a methodological principle stated in the Discussion.

claim: Visual and olfactory memories share the same subsets of dopamine neurons that convey reinforcing signals.
source: We found that visual and olfactory memories share the same subsets of dopamine neurons that convey reinforcing signals (Figures 2,3 and 4).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by data in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Shared requirement of the transmitter system between visual and olfactory learning has been described in crickets.
source: This shared requirement of the transmitter system between visual and olfactory learning has been described in crickets (Unoki et al., 2005, 2006; Mizunami et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in crickets.

claim: For electric shock reinforcement, identified neurons in the PPL1 cluster (MB-MP1, MB-MV1, MB-V1) drive aversive memories in both visual and olfactory learning.
source: For electric shock reinforcement, identified neurons in the PPL1 cluster, such as MB-MP1, MB-MV1 and MB-V1, drive aversive memories in both visual and olfactory learning (Figures 3F and 4C; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2010, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figures 3F and 4C and citations to prior work.

claim: The MB-M3 neurons in the PAM cluster seem to be involved specifically in aversive olfactory memory.
source: while the MB-M3 neurons in the PAM cluster seem to be involved specifically in aversive olfactory memory (Figure 2A, data not shown) (Aso et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A and citations to prior work.

claim: Overlapping sets of dopamine neurons appear to represent electric shock punishment in both visual and olfactory learning with olfactory aversive memory probably recruiting a larger set.
source: Thus, overlapping sets of dopamine neurons appear to represent electric shock punishment in both visual and olfactory learning with olfactory aversive memory probably recruiting a larger set.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential dopamine neuron requirements.

claim: The MB-M3 neurons induce aversive olfactory memory that increases stability of other memory components.
source: We previously showed that the MB-M3 neurons induce aversive olfactory memory that increases stability of other memory components (Aso et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Olfactory memories last longer than visual memories.
source: Olfactory memories last longer than visual memories (data not shown; Schnaitmann et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data and citation to prior work.

claim: PAM cluster neurons play crucial roles in both olfactory and visual appetitive memories.
source: In appetitive conditioning, PAM cluster neurons play crucial roles in both olfactory and visual memories (Figure 2A,D,E, Figure 3C,E, Figure 4B; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in multiple figures and citations to prior work.

claim: All dopamine neurons conveying reinforcement signals project to restricted subdomains of the mushroom body.
source: Most importantly, all these neurons convey dopamine signals to restricted subdomains of the MB.
evidence: This is an anatomical observation based on the expression patterns shown in Figure 3.

claim: The blockade of octopamine neurons did not impair appetitive visual memories with sucrose.
source: The blockade of octopamine neurons did not impair appetitive visual memories with sucrose (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The involvement of octopamine neurons may be more substantial when non-nutritious sweet taste rewards are used, as has been shown in olfactory learning.
source: The involvement of octopamine neurons may be more substantial when non-nutritious sweet taste rewards are used, as has been shown in olfactory learning (Burke et al., 2012).
evidence: This speculation is supported by citation to prior work in olfactory learning.

claim: The necessity of mushroom body output for visual memory acquisition and retrieval is consistent with olfactory conditioning.
source: In addition to these shared reinforcement circuits in the MB, the necessity of MB output for visual memory acquisition and retrieval is also consistent with olfactory conditioning (Figure 8; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Schwaerzel et al., 2002; Krashes et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 8 and citations to prior work on olfactory conditioning.

claim: The recruited Kenyon cell subsets are not identical for visual and olfactory modalities.
source: although the recruited KC subsets are not identical for different modalities (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mushroom bodies harbor associative plasticity for visual memories.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the MBs harbor associative plasticity for visual memories
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental findings.

claim: Similar coincidence detection mechanisms are used to form memories within the mushroom bodies.
source: and support the conclusion that similar coincidence detection mechanisms are used to form memories within the MBs (Figure 9) (Heisenberg, 2003; Gerber et al., 2004b; Qin et al., 2012).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the experimental findings and citations to prior work.

claim: Centralization of similar brain functions spares the cost of maintaining similar circuit motifs in different brain areas and may be an evolutionary conserved design of information processing.
source: Centralization of similar brain functions spares the cost of maintaining similar circuit motifs in different brain areas and may be an evolutionary conserved design of information processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Converging inputs of different stimuli into a multisensory area have been described in humans.
source: Such converging inputs of different stimuli into a multisensory area have even been described in humans (Beauchamp et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in humans.

claim: Flight simulator visual learning was shown to require the central complex but not the mushroom bodies.
source: 'Flight simulator' visual learning was shown to require the central complex but not the MBs (Wolf et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2006; Pan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work using the flight simulator.

claim: There are important differences between the flight simulator paradigm and the visual learning assay used in this study.
source: Although this appears to contradict our study, we note that there are important differences between the behavioral paradigms employed.
evidence: This is an observation about methodological differences.

claim: Flies during flight show octopamine-mediated modulation of neurons in the optic lobe.
source: Given that flies during flight show octopamine-mediated modulation of neurons in the optic lobe (Suver et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: State-dependent mechanisms might underlie different requirement of higher brain centers in different behavioral paradigms.
source: similar state-dependent mechanisms might underlie different requirement of higher brain centers.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the discrepancy with flight simulator studies.

claim: The role of the mushroom body in associative learning is not restricted to one sensory modality or reinforcer.
source: This study together with the results in associative taste learning (Masek and Scott, 2010; Keene and Masek, 2012) highlights the fact that the role of the MB in associative learning is not restricted to one sensory modality or reinforcer (Figure 9).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the current findings and citations to prior work on taste learning.

claim: Olfactory and visual memories recruit overlapping, yet partly distinct, sets of Kenyon cells.
source: We found that olfactory and visual memories recruit overlapping, yet partly distinct, sets of Kenyon cells (Figures 6,9).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Visual inputs to the mushroom body remain unidentified.
source: In contrast to the well-described olfactory projection neurons, visual inputs to the MB remain unidentified.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: No anatomical evidence has been reported in Drosophila for direct connections between optic lobes and mushroom bodies.
source: No anatomical evidence has been reported in Drosophila for direct connections between optic lobes and MBs (Otsuna and Ito, 2006; Mu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Direct connections between optic lobes and mushroom bodies are found in other insects.
source: although such connections are found in other insects (Mobbs, 1982; Schildberger, 1984; Li and Strausfeld, 1997; Gronenberg and Hölldobler, 1999; Paulk and Gronenberg, 2008; Lin and Strausfeld, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in other insect species.

claim: Afferents originating in the protocerebrum were found to provide multi-modal input to the mushroom body lobes of cockroaches.
source: Also afferents originating in the protocerebrum were found to provide multi-modal input to the MB lobes of cockroaches (Li and Strausfeld, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in cockroaches.

claim: Drosophila mushroom bodies may receive indirect visual input from optic lobes.
source: Thus, Drosophila MBs may receive indirect visual input from optic lobes
evidence: This is a speculation based on findings in other insects.

claim: Visual and olfactory cues may be both represented in the γ neurons.
source: Given the general requirement of the γ lobe neurons (Figure 7), visual and olfactory cues may be both represented in the γ neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement of γ lobe neurons shown in Figure 7.

claim: The dopamine neurons that convey appetitive and aversive memories heavily project to the γ lobe.
source: Consistently, the dopamine neurons that convey appetitive and aversive memories heavily project to the γ lobe (Figure 3A,B; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2010, 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data in Figure 3 and citations to prior work.

claim: In olfactory conditioning, the γ lobe was shown to contribute mainly to short-term memory.
source: In olfactory conditioning, the γ lobe was shown to contribute mainly to short-term memory (Zars et al., 2000; Isabel et al., 2004; Blum et al., 2009; Trannoy et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on olfactory memory.

claim: Converging evidence from olfactory and visual memories suggests a general role for the γ lobe in short-lasting memories across different sensory modalities.
source: This converging evidence from olfactory and visual memories suggests a general role for the γ lobe in short-lasting memories across different sensory modalities (Figures 6,7 and 9).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the current findings and prior work on olfactory memory.

claim: The mushroom body is involved in sensorimotor gating of visual stimuli or visual selective attention.
source: Previous studies found that the MB is also involved in sensorimotor gating of visual stimuli or visual selective attention (van Swinderen and Greenspan, 2003; Xi et al., 2008; van Swinderen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mushroom body circuits for visual associative memories might be required for sensorimotor gating and attention.
source: Therefore, the MB circuits for visual associative memories might be required for sensorimotor gating and attention.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior findings about MB function.
